newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Foreign banks can deal with new Manila forex rules.
newsitem.headline: Foreign banks can deal with new Manila forex rules.

text.p: Foreign banks operating in Manila said on Tuesday they could cope with new controls on their behaviour which are meant to ease pressure on the embattled peso.
"The foreign banks should be able to work within these new guidelines," ING Bank country manager Renato de Guzman told Reuters.
"We're in an abnormal situation right now. That's why we have this type of solution," he added.
The Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) recommended on Monday the exclusion of foreign banks from the spot foreign exchange market to reduce demand for the U.S. currency.
The BAP operates the Philippine dealing system, through which most banks do their onshore currency trading.
It was the latest move by Manila to curb speculation and reduce pressure on the peso after its effective devaluation on July 11.
Foreign banks are now forced to buy their dollars from the central bank through forward contracts of up to 90 days.
"As long as the forward rates are reasonable, we can work with that," de Guzman added.
Last week, the central bank, also upon the suggestion of the BAP, temporarily suspended the sale of forward dollars on a non-delivery basis.

"To a certain extent, these may go against the free market policy. It may be a vicissitude of the free market development, but it's a positive development," Antonio Agcaoili, treasurer of Banco Santander in Manila, said.
He said the measures had helped ease uncertainties in the market.
"Before that, everything was in a state of flux. Exporters were holding on to their dollars," Agcaoili said.
The peso-dollar market has normalised after the new guideline was announced on Monday, with turnover rising to a more usual $114.8 million from the previous $10-40 million daily turnover last week.
The parallel market rate, which has been more market determined due to the absence of central bank intervention, was now hewing closer to the official rate.
The peso was hovering between 28.50 and 29.00 on Monday from the range of 29.00-29.50 last Friday. The peso closed in the official market on Tuesday at 28.5 pesos per dollar.
Agcaoili said the new guidelines are the lesser of the two evils.
Without them, the peso-dollar market might remain very thin and make the peso more vulnerable to fresh attacks, he added.
Other bankers were less sanguine, saying the local monetary authorities may be going too far in restricting development of the market.
"These are just cosmetic remedies. What the central bank should do is to let go of the rate some more and the speculators will leave the peso alone," a trader at a foreign bank said.
He suggested that the peso should be allowed to float to 29.00 to 29.50 which he thought was its true value.
Central Bank deputy governor Alberto Reyes said the measures were just temporary, and no other restrictions were being studied.
